Record any real conversation and write it down, and the first thing you notice is how little of it consists of complete sentences. People say: coffee? And the answer is: please. They say: I haven't, but she has. And nobody asks what it is that she has done. Learners are taught to answer in full. Yes, I would like some coffee, thank you. It is grammatically perfect, and it sounds like somebody filling in a form. The reason is simple. Every time you repeat words that both of you already have, you are telling your listener that you do not trust them to remember. Leaving words out is a quiet act of trust. That is why ellipsis feels warm, and why full sentences, in the wrong place, feel cold. The rule I give my students is short. Say only the part that is new. Everything else, your listener already has.

I teach young doctors, and with them I argue the opposite. At a handover, when one team passes its patients to the next, ellipsis is dangerous. Did he have the second dose? He did. Which patient? Which dose? At three in the morning, the person listening fills in the gaps, and sometimes fills them in wrongly. So we ask for complete sentences, with names and numbers, even when it sounds stiff and even when everybody is tired. It is not that leaving words out is bad English. It is that it depends on shared context, and shared context is exactly what you cannot assume about someone who has just started a shift. At dinner, leave things out. When somebody else is going to act on what you said, spell it out.
